title: Gas Prices Drop in June, But Experts Say the Relief Won’t Last
summary: Have you noticed the price at the pump lately? In June, filling up your family car got a little cheaper. The average price for a gallon of gas dropped to $3.85—down from $4.07 just a month ago. That’s because oil prices fell when it looked like the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil tankers, might stay open. Overall, what people pay for things like food and rent also rose more slowly in June. But here’s the catch: that good news might be short-lived. A ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran fell apart last week, and tankers were attacked. Since then, gas prices have already started climbing again. One expert says $4 gas could be just days away, and diesel might hit $5. The White House had celebrated the drop, saying it proved that peace in the strait would make inflation “plummet like a rock.” But now, with fighting back on, those savings could vanish. The Federal Reserve, which helps control inflation, is under pressure to keep prices stable. For now, markets are up, but families might feel the pinch again soon.
why_it_matters: When gas prices rise, it can affect how much money your family has for other things, like food or fun activities.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that connects the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea.
About one-fifth of the world's oil passes through this strait, so any trouble there can quickly affect fuel prices all over the world.
The Federal Reserve (the U.S. central bank) works to keep inflation—the rate at which prices rise—under control, but it cannot directly stop oil price shocks.

perspectives.description: Lower gas prices help families save money on travel and daily needs.
The relief is only temporary, and the return of fighting could make prices even higher than before.
This shows how events in faraway places, like a narrow strait, can quickly change what people pay at the pump.
